show: Germans de sang (Catalan-language production of Willy Russell's musical Blood Brothers, Teatre Condal, Barcelona)
synopsis:
Mrs. Johnstone gives birth to twin boys while already struggling to feed her many children after their father abandons the family. When she takes cleaning work for the wealthy Sra. Lyons, the childless woman persuades her to give up one of the babies. Sra. Lyons raises the child as Eddie Lyons, while Mrs. Johnstone keeps Mickey Johnstone, and the brothers grow up unaware of one another’s existence. Haunted by fear that the truth will emerge, Sra. Lyons binds Mrs. Johnstone with a superstition: if twins separated at birth ever learn they were once a pair, both will die at once.

As boys, Mickey and Eddie meet by chance and become inseparable. They solemnly cut their hands and swear to be “blood brothers,” even though their mothers desperately try to separate them. Eddie’s family moves away, but years later he returns and renews the friendship. By then the two young men have also fallen for Linda. She chooses Mickey, and their marriage initially promises a way forward, while Eddie leaves to pursue education and a successful public career.

Mickey’s prospects collapse as work disappears and poverty tightens around his family. Pressured by Sammy, he joins a robbery that goes disastrously wrong; a man is shot, and Mickey is imprisoned. On his release he is traumatised, dependent on medication, unemployed, and convinced that Linda and Eddie have betrayed him. Sra. Lyons goads him by suggesting Linda and Eddie are lovers, and when Mrs. Johnstone finally blurts out the secret of the twins’ birth, the truth arrives too late: armed and desperate, Mickey confronts Eddie, and both brothers are killed in the ensuing tragedy.

The show turns a bond formed in childhood into a devastating question of whether lives are shaped by fate or by social class. It exposes how inequality, poverty, fear, and withheld truth can destroy family love, while the brothers’ shared blood makes the division between their worlds painfully artificial.

show: Los chicos del coro, el musical (Spanish stage-musical adaptation of the French film Les Choristes, Teatre Tivoli Barcelona / Madrid)
synopsis:
Pepin waits at the gates of El Fondo del Estanque, watching for the father who never comes, when Clément Mathieu arrives to take up work at the bleak boarding school. A composer whose own career came to nothing, taken on as a substitute teacher, Mathieu finds boys branded as troublesome, abandoned or beyond reform, living under the harsh authority of the director, Sr. Rachin. Rachin rules through “acción–reacción”: every prank, failure or defiance earns an immediate punishment. The boys answer this regime with mischief, anger and distrust, while Maxence, the school’s caretaker, quietly offers Mathieu his first welcome.

Instead of accepting Rachin’s verdict on the pupils, Mathieu notices their energy, their loneliness and their untapped ability. He begins to write music and secretly gathers them into a choir, assigning voices and teaching them to listen to one another. Pepín’s longing, the defiance of Pierre Morhange, and the different wounds carried by the other boys gradually find an outlet in rehearsal. Pierre, whose gift for singing is exceptional, is being raised alone by his mother, Violette Morhange, and it is Mathieu who first makes her hear what her son can do.

Mathieu’s work is challenged when Rachin treats the choir as a threat to discipline rather than a chance for change. Help arrives from the forthright profesora Langlois, who heads a nearby girls’ school; after an accident there she and her pupils are billeted at El Fondo del Estanque, and the girls’ arrival makes Rachin’s regime look not merely cruel but faintly ridiculous. But the arrival of Mondain, an older boy with a dark baritone and darker history, intensifies the school’s tensions and gives Rachin another excuse to impose fear.

Against repeated setbacks, the choir learns trust, responsibility and pride. Its growing success not only gives the children a voice but also challenges the bleak future that El Fondo del Estanque has assigned them.

The musical centres on the restorative force of art, compassion and patient education in the lives of neglected children. It contrasts punishment with understanding, showing how solidarity and recognition can turn isolation and anger into hope.

show: Mentiras, el musical (landmark Mexican jukebox musical of 1980s Spanish-language hits, Teatro Aldama, Mexico City)
synopsis:
At Emmanuel’s funeral, Daniela, Dulce, Yuri and Lupita arrive expecting to mourn the same charming, affluent man—only to discover that each believed herself to be his one true love. The shock deepens when the elegant, enigmatic Manoela presents Emmanuel’s final message: his death was no accident, and the woman responsible must be one of the four women gathered in the house.

Trapped together by suspicion, grief and outrage, the women begin to reconstruct Emmanuel’s elaborate web of deceptions. Daniela, whose picture-perfect domestic world has suddenly collapsed, confronts the possibility that her marriage was built on illusion. Yuri, fiery and self-possessed, refuses to be dismissed as merely another betrayed lover. Lupita, the long-suffering secretary whose job gave her intimate access to Emmanuel’s private life, recalls what she saw and swallowed, while Dulce’s story adds yet another version of the man each woman thought she knew. Their testimonies contradict, overlap and expose jealousies, concealed ambitions and old wounds.

As accusations fly, Emmanuel’s past emerges in fragments: promises made to different women, identities adjusted to suit each romance, and a carefully maintained fiction that kept them all apart. The investigation forces Daniela, Dulce, Yuri and Lupita to look beyond their rivalry and question the roles Emmanuel assigned them. By the time the truth surrounding his death comes into focus, the women must decide whether to remain prisoners of his lies or reclaim the authority to tell their own stories.

The show turns betrayal into a comic, high-stakes mystery while examining romantic illusion, female friendship and self-determination. Its central question is not only who deceived whom, but how the women rebuild themselves once the fantasy of Emmanuel is gone.

show: Pegados, un musical diferente (award-winning original Spanish musical comedy premiered 2010, winner of three Premis Butaca and two Premios Max, Gran Teatro Pavon Madrid)
synopsis:
In the bathroom of a nightclub, a chico and a chica give in to the momentum of a night fuelled by music, drink and attraction. What ought to be a fleeting anonymous encounter takes an absurd turn when, at its end, they discover that they are physically unable to separate. After a series of increasingly desperate, unsuccessful attempts to free themselves, embarrassment and panic leave them with only one practical option: go to Urgencias.

Installed together on a hospital bed, still literally pegados, the two strangers face an ordeal neither can escape. The doctor is nowhere to be found, and the nurse who remains with them seems remarkably unmoved by their predicament. Worse still, the wait stretches on. The doctor will not arrive until the end, because he is also the show’s pianist: abandoning the piano would bring the musical itself to a halt. Trapped by circumstance and by their shared body, the chico and chica have no choice but to talk.

Their enforced intimacy turns the hospital room into a comic battleground. They try to protect their dignity, account for the humiliating accident and negotiate the practical problems of being joined together, while their initial assumptions about one another begin to unravel. Irritation, shame, defensiveness and curiosity give way to candid exchanges as they learn who the other person is beyond the hurried encounter in the discoteca. Songs punctuate their long confinement, transforming an awkward medical emergency into a wildly theatrical waiting game.

At its heart, Pegados, un musical diferente turns physical entrapment into a comic test of emotional openness. It plays with the gap between sexual proximity and genuine intimacy, asking what can happen when two people are forced to stop running from connection.

show: Autonomos, el musical (Catalan-language comedy musical about freelancers by Alex Martinez Vidal, Andreu Rami and Joan Berenguer, Espai Texas Barcelona)
synopsis:
In a not-too-distant future, the economic crisis has ended, every citizen holds a stable job, and happiness is all but guaranteed. Àlex is living that promise. That security collapses without warning when he is dismissed. Left clutching his mobile phone and with no clear path back into conventional work, he has to take charge of his own survival. Becoming an autònom—a freelance self-employed worker—emerges as the only available option.

His attempt to build a livelihood quickly turns into a frantic initiation into a world whose promises of independence conceal an obstacle course. He must find work, make himself marketable, and keep moving through an unstable labour market while also confronting the pressures of housing and everyday expenses. Each apparent solution brings another demand: the motivational rhetoric of an entrepreneurship guru urges him to turn uncertainty into ambition, while the Agència Tributària represents the relentless bureaucracy and financial obligations that accompany self-employment. A highly individual gestor offers assistance, but navigating the rules and responsibilities of this new working life remains anything but simple: simply registering as self-employed means facing a clerk and a bureaucracy in which every step demands three separate forms.

As Àlex tries to reinvent himself, his ordeal is shared, challenged and amplified by the friend who goes through it beside him. Their friendship becomes a practical refuge amid setbacks, absurd encounters, and the constant need to improvise. Together, they confront a system in which “being your own boss” can mean being pursued by clients, bills, administrative deadlines, and the expectation that every personal difficulty should be solved with optimism. Songs transform those pressures into comic episodes, but the story never lets Àlex forget the precariousness beneath the jokes: every small victory must be earned, and every month must somehow be made to add up.

The musical turns freelance work into an adventure of resilience, friendship, and self-reinvention. Its comedy exposes the gap between entrepreneurial fantasy and the economic, bureaucratic, and emotional realities of trying to survive independently.

show: Un refugi al sol (Catalan-language small-format original musical by Cia Geminis, Sala Versus Glories Barcelona)
synopsis:
Kai and Ària are the Heliogàbal siblings, a pop duo about to compete at the Benidorm Fest with a song in Catalan and their eyes on Eurovision. Days before the contest their bond fractures: Kai, unable to help his new boyfriend when it mattered most, is left so wounded that he disappears, and Ària ends up singing in Benidorm alone. He retreats to Mas Soler, the family farmhouse in the Pallars Jussà. There he finds his padrina, Dolors — a retired chemistry teacher and village healer who talks to the dead and keeps a house she says is never empty of spirits. Outside, a fascism that spreads like a virus has the country shutting itself indoors; everywhere, at least, except the Benidorm stage. Dolors refuses to let Kai cut himself off from the people and places that made him: stories that are not told, she warns him, are forgotten.

At Mas Soler, comic rural myths, queer legends and supernatural encounters—including a trencalòs with human legs that serves as the show’s magical deus ex machina—disturb Kai’s isolation and turn refuge into confrontation. Dolors guides him through journeys across time and into a biscuit tin holding the real wartime diary his oncle avi wrote after going to the Republican front at seventeen: another young man, adrift amid violence and uncertainty, becomes an unsettling reflection of Kai’s own disorientation. The family’s history challenges him to see that withdrawal cannot protect him from the forces reshaping the present. Ària, through to the next round in Benidorm, comes back for her brother, and the siblings’ differing ways of facing crisis return to the surface. With Dolors’s old chemistry proving unexpectedly decisive, Kai must decide whether he can return to performance not as an escape or a bid for success, but as the act that might speak to a frightened generation.

The musical frames identity as something forged between private hurt, inherited memory and collective resistance. It celebrates queer self-expression, rural voices and intergenerational solidarity while warning against the return of fascism in new forms.
